Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

vignette: Akua's eyes would glaze over whenever she found herself near large bodies of water. The sight of waves or even a flooded street would transport her back to the dimly lit cell where she was held captive and tortured. She remembered the feeling of being submerged in icy cold water, unable to breathe, and the sound of her own screams muffled by the darkness. Her body would tense up, assuming the same position as when she was bound and helpless. These moments were always fragmented, like pieces of a puzzle she couldn't quite assemble - an incomplete picture that left her with more questions than answers. Akua's relationship with her partner, Kwame, had become strained since her return from captivity. Arguments would trigger memories of the verbal abuse she suffered at the hands of her captors. She began to avoid confrontations, not just with Kwame but also with colleagues at the pharmacy where she worked. Avoiding conflicts meant avoiding people who reminded her of those involved in the event or even individuals who shared similar features - a cruel irony given that her role as a pharmacist required empathy and communication. Akua would tell herself that she deserved to suffer, that she was lucky to have survived while others did not. This self-imposed punishment thinking made it difficult for her to shake off feelings of guilt whenever she thought about the event. Her hypervigilance had become a constant companion - always on guard, scanning her surroundings for potential threats, and planning escape routes in case of an emergency. Sleep became a luxury as she struggled to fall asleep due to her need to remain alert. Akua found it challenging to articulate her experiences, often getting stuck on the sensation of water or the feeling of being trapped without being able to verbalize what happened. Her memories were visceral - reliving the sensations in her body whenever they resurfaced. These bodily reenactments left her breathless and disoriented. As time passed, Akua started avoiding situations that might trigger nightmares - late nights, certain movies, or even conversations about her past. She became withdrawn, using avoidance as a maladaptive strategy to cope with the pain of remembering. Her partner, Kwame, began to notice changes in her behavior and encouraged her to seek help. Akua's perception of herself had become distorted; she believed that thinking about the event would be too overwhelming to handle. This thought avoidance led her to suppress emotions, creating a sense of numbness that extended beyond her memories. Her guilt for surviving when others did not manifested as self-blame and self-punishment - further solidifying her maladaptive coping mechanisms. Her world had shrunk, and everyday situations became minefields waiting to be triggered. The threat of being overwhelmed by memories or emotions was ever-present, making it difficult for Akua to distinguish between past and present. As she navigated this treacherous landscape, the cycle of avoidance, guilt, and hypervigilance continued to reinforce itself. It wasn't until Kwame staged an intervention that Akua finally realized she needed help breaking free from this cycle. With his support, she took the first tentative steps towards seeking therapy - a daunting prospect for someone who had become accustomed to self-imposed silence. As she sat in her therapist's office, Akua whispered, "I don't know if I can do this... what if remembering is too much?"
